paper_title: What Generation Knows: Unlocking Fine-Grained Understanding in Unified Multimodal Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Fine-grained visual understanding requires distinguishing subtle differences in local attributes and spatial relations, yet remains challenging for existing vision-language models. Unified multimodal models (UMMs) offer a new opportunity through generation pathways that preserve rich visual information complementary to understanding. However, existing generation-assisted understanding methods mainly rely on generative supervision or explicit generation and have not systematically explored direct use of native generation-side representations. To address this gap, we systematically analyze what generation-side representations offer for fine-grained understanding, finding that they are more sensitive to fine-grained semantic changes, capture task-relevant changes missed by understanding-side representations, and depend on correct spatial organization for this advantage. Guided by these findings, we design GAFU, a post-training framework that unlocks native generation-side information for fine-grained understanding. It compresses generation-side visual representations into compact \(G\) tokens that preserve fine-grained visual details, enabling task-conditioned retrieval by the understanding pathway. Experiments show that GAFU consistently outperforms SFT baselines trained on the same data across diverse visual understanding tasks and UMM architectures, with maximum relative improvements of 20.00\%, 17.94\%, and 8.62\% on VStar-Bench, OmniSpatial, and VSR-Bench, respectively. Overall, GAFU converts complementary information from the generation pathway into gains in fine-grained visual understanding, providing an effective path toward synergy between generation and understanding in UMMs.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: In recent years, vision-language models (VLMs) have made substantial progress in visual understanding (Li et al., 2024a; Bai et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2025). However, this progress remains uneven between high-level semantic understanding and fine-grained visual understanding: while VLMs are comparatively strong in high-level semantic understanding, they remain substantially less reliable on fine-grained tasks involving objects, attributes, counting, and spatial relations (Tong et al., 2024b; Fu et al., 2024; Kamoi et al., 2025). Existing methods mainly improve fine-grained visual understanding through higher-fidelity visual encoding and more information-preserving visionlanguage interfaces (You et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024b; Tong et al., 2024a; Zhang et al., 2025), but still rely on language-aligned vision encoders that compress visual content into limited representations before language modeling, so that fine-grained evidence lost upstream becomes unavailable downstream. UMMs jointly model multimodal understanding and generation within single model (Team, 2025; Zhao et al., 2026). Compared with VLMs that rely primarily on language-aligned visual representations, the generation pathway in UMMs typically preserves richer structural information, spatial relations, and local details (Wu et al., 2025a; Qu et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2025a). Meanwhile, the understanding and generation pathways share knowledge and mutually adapt during joint modeling, 1 providing basis for complementary use of the two types of visual information (Deng et al., 2025; Kang et al., 2026). However, fine-grained visual understanding remains challenging for UMMs, and it remains unclear whether and under what conditions generation-side representations provide additional evidence for fine-grained understanding, as well as how such evidence can be effectively exploited by the understanding pathway (Liu et al., 2026a; Wang et al., 2026; Wen et al., 2026). Generation-assisted understanding in UMMs mainly follows two directions. One line uses generative supervision to shape visual representations or internal hidden states to encode richer fine-grained visual information (Wang et al., 2024b; Luo et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2024a). However, these methods do not directly examine or exploit information in native generation-side representations. Their heuristic supervision targets limit task-conditioned visual evidence selection, while differing representational requirements of understanding and generation may introduce representational conflicts (Ma et al., 2025b; Chen et al., 2025a; Su et al., 2026). Another line explicitly generates visual intermediate states at inference time and uses them for downstream understanding (Su et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025). However, this approach externalizes generation-side information into limited intermediate states, with some methods re-encoding the outputs into the understanding space and reintroducing the visual encoding bottleneck of the understanding pathway (Cheng et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026; Hao et al., 2026; Cheng et al., 2026). Explicit generation introduces inference overhead and may propagate generation errors into downstream understanding (Meng et al., 2026). To address these limitations, we first examine how generation-side representations contribute to finegrained understanding. We focus on whether they contain visual cues beyond those captured by the understanding pathway and on the factors that determine this advantage. We find that generationside representations respond more strongly to subtle semantic changes, capture changes missed by understanding-side representations, and rely on spatial organization to retain this advantage. Guided by these findings, we propose GAFU, Generation-Assisted Fine-grained Understanding post-training framework that directly exploits native generation-side representations. To preserve fine-grained information, GAFU transforms native generation-side representations into compact tokens through compression, spatial binding, and relation alignment. We then use the evolving text states to selectively retrieve task-relevant evidence from and feed it back into the understanding pathway. We further use pairwise preference learning to encourage reliance on sample-relevant generation-side evidence while preserving the original understanding capability. We evaluate GAFU across UMMs with diverse architectures and scales on general, spatial, and domain-specific visual understanding tasks. GAFU outperforms same-data SFT in all 15 modelbenchmark combinations, with substantial average gains of 3.565.98 percentage points across the five benchmarks. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: 1. We systematically study understandingand generation-side visual representations in UMMs, revealing generation-side advantages in fine-grained semantic sensitivity, representational complementarity, and spatial dependence. 2. Based on these findings, we propose GAFU, which enables the understanding pathway to exploit complementary generation-side information through representation compression and alignment, task-conditioned injection, and pairwise preference learning. 3. We validate GAFU across diverse UMM architectures and visual understanding tasks, outperforming same-data SFT in all 15 settings by 3.565.98 percentage points on average.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: 2.1 UNIFIED MULTIMODAL MODELS UMMs jointly model multimodal understanding and visual generation within single model through autoregressive, diffusion-based, or hybrid modeling paradigms (Wang et al., 2024c; Xie et al., 2025a; You et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026). Early UMMs often relied on unified dense backbone with shared visual representations (Team, 2025; Wang et al., 2024c), while later designs increasingly specialize the visual pathways for understanding and generation within unified framework (Wu et al., 2025a; Fu et al., 2026). This evolution reflects different representation needs: understanding relies more on high-level semantics, whereas generation requires richer visual details, motivating many UMMs to use language-aligned encoders such as CLIP or SigLIP for understanding and 2 VAEor VQ-VAE-based encoders for generation (Wu et al., 2025a;b; Fu et al., 2026). Despite this progress, architectural unification has not yet translated into effective synergy between understanding and generation (Shi et al., 2026), with persistent capability gaps (Wang et al., 2026) and limited generation-to-understanding transfer (Wen et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2026).

sections.title: 2.2 UNDERSTANDING–GENERATION COLLABORATION IN UNIFIED MULTIMODAL MODELS
sections.content: Collaboration between understanding and generation in UMMs mainly follows two directions: understanding-guided generation and generation-assisted understanding. Understanding-guided generation uses understanding-side information for generation conditioning (Dong et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025b; Xie et al., 2026), task planning (Zeng et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026b; Li et al., 2026), and output feedback (Jin et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026b), forming relatively mature paradigm. In contrast, generation-assisted understanding has received comparatively less systematic attention. It mainly relies on generative supervision to shape visual representations or internal states (Wang et al., 2024b; Ma et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2024a), which can constrain representation learning through indirect objectives, or on generated visual intermediate states (Li et al., 2025; Tong et al., 2026; Hao et al., 2026), which introduce costly and lossy intermediate generation process (Meng et al., 2026). However, the role of native generation-side representations in understanding remains underexplored, particularly whether they provide complementary evidence, what enables such advantages, and how they can be used effectively.

sections.title: 3.2 GENERATION-ASSISTED UNDERSTANDING FRAMEWORK
sections.content: Our analysis reveals complementary generation-side evidence whose advantage depends on spatial organization and varies across tasks. GAFU accordingly preserves and aligns this information in compact tokens and enables task-conditioned retrieval by the understanding pathway.

sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: 4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP Data. We train the compression and alignment module on 1M images from Cambrian (Tong et al., 2024a). For downstream fine-tuning, we use FineVision (Wiedmann et al., 2026), Visual Spatial Reasoning (VSR) (Liu et al., 2023), and PathVQA (He et al., 2020) for general and domain-specific understanding. Detailed data composition and preprocessing are provided in Appendix D. Models and Training. We experiment on three UMMs, BAGEL (Deng et al., 2025), JanusPro (Chen et al., 2025c), and Lance (Fu et al., 2026). During compression and alignment, we freeze the native pathways and optimize the Encoder, Decoder, and prediction heads. During task-conditioned fine-tuning, we optimize the injection modules and understanding-pathway LoRA adapters, with the compression Encoder later unfrozen for joint optimization. Training configurations and hyperparameters are provided in Appendix D. Evaluation. For general fine-grained visual understanding, we evaluate on VStar-Bench, OmniSpatial, and MMVP, covering fine-grained visual perception and spatial understanding. For domainspecific evaluation, we report results on VSR-Bench and PathVQA. We compare against the Base model and SFT baselines trained on the same data. Evaluation details are provided in Appendix D. 4.2 GENERAL FINE-GRAINED VISUAL UNDERSTANDING We evaluate whether GAFU provides consistent gains beyond SFT for general fine-grained visual understanding across UMM architectures. As shown in Table 1, GAFU outperforms SFT on all three benchmarks across BAGEL, Janus-Pro, and Lance, improving VStar-Bench by 5.237.85 percentage points, OmniSpatial by 2.614.44 points, and MMVP by 3.675.67 points. The consistent gains from 3B Lance to 14B BAGEL show that generation-side complementarity benefits fine-grained visual understanding across model scales, UMM architectures, and representation pathways. Across all nine modelbenchmark combinations, the improvement of our method over SFT is larger than that of SFT over the Base model. This contrast is particularly evident on MMVP, where SFT brings no improvement to Janus-Pro and slightly degrades Lance, whereas our method achieves further gains, suggesting that supervised adaptation relying solely on the native understanding pathway cannot reliably overcome its fine-grained visual representation bottleneck, while complementary generation-side information provides additional effective visual evidence. sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We present GAFU, generation-assisted understanding post-training framework for fine-grained visual understanding in UMMs. First, we systematically examine the role of native generationside representations in fine-grained understanding and the conditions that enable it. Second, based on these findings, GAFU preserves and organizes complementary generation-side information through compression, spatial binding, and relation alignment, selectively retrieves it through task-conditioned injection, and promotes the use of sample-relevant evidence through pairwise preference learning. Third, across UMM architectures, GAFU consistently outperforms same-data SFT on general, spatial, and domain-specific visual understanding tasks, with maximum relative gains of 20.00%, 17.94%, and 8.62% on VStar-Bench, OmniSpatial, and VSR-Bench, respectively. Overall, GAFU converts complementary information in native generation-side representations into usable visual evidence for the understanding pathway, yielding consistent gains in fine-grained visual understanding. We hope this work will help UMMs move beyond joint modeling of understanding and generation toward deeper capability synergy, and provide new path toward more reliable and fine-grained visual understanding in complex real-world scenarios.

sections.content: This work uses existing datasets and benchmark suites, including Cambrian, FineVision, VStarBench, OmniSpatial, MMVP, VSR-Bench, VisMin, and PathVQA, for model training and evaluation, in accordance with their respective data-use and citation requirements. The medical questionanswering results on PathVQA are intended solely for research benchmarking and should not be used to support clinical decisions. This work does not involve privacy-sensitive data, human subjects, new data collection, dataset release, or the development of potentially harmful insights. The authors declare no conflicts of interest or external sponsorship related to this work.

sections.title: REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT
sections.content: For reproducing the systematic analysis: Section 3.1 introduces the overall setup, research questions, and analysis procedure. Appendix further specifies the extraction and preprocessing of understandingand generation-side representations across UMMs, together with the computation of the sensitivity, resolution, and spatial-dependence analyses. For reproducing GAFU training and evaluation: Section 3.2 describes the overall GAFU architecture and the basic procedures of Stage 1 and Stage 2, while Section 4.1 summarizes the tasks, models, and overall experimental setup. Appendix specifies the Stage 1 GToken EncoderDecoder architecture and the computation of the reconstruction, spatial-binding, and relation-alignment objectives. Appendix describes the Stage 2 injection modules, training objectives, gradient decomposition, masking schedule, and shuffle-donor construction. Appendix provides the data composition, preprocessing examples, optimizer and training configurations, and evaluation protocols.

sections.content: A.1 REPRESENTATION EXTRACTION AND PREPROCESSING We extract the understanding-side representation RU and generation-side representation RG from each UMM as follows: BAGEL. RU comprises the SigLIP visual tokens after the connector (16 16). RG is obtained from the KL-VAE posterior mean (64 64) through 2 2 patchification, yielding 32 32 grid. Janus-Pro. RU comprises the SigLIP-L/16 visual tokens after the aligner, and RG comprises the quantized VQ-16 codebook embeddings Qvq, both on 24 24 grids. Lance. RU comprises the merged Qwen visual tokens (16 16), and RG is the posterior mean of the frozen Wan2.2-VAE (32 32). Show-o2-7B. RU is extracted from the output of image embedder und after adding the native visual positional embedding and applying und trans. RG is extracted from the output of image embedder gen. Both representations are adaptively average-pooled to common 16 16 grid. The resulting channel dimensions are 1152 for RU and 3584 for RG. BLIP3-o-4B. RU comprises the merged Qwen2.5-VL visual tokens (16 16), and RG comprises the penultimate-layer patch features of the EVA-CLIP-E/14-plus generation vision tower (32 32). DreamLLM-7B. RU comprises the penultimate-layer CLIP ViT-L/14 patch features after the native projector, excluding the CLS token (1616). RG is the generation VAE posterior mean with the native latent scaling factor applied (64 64). We preserve the spatial arrangement of each representation and align its grid to 16 16 using adaptive average pooling, yielding the position-wise features R(I, p) used in the main text. For VAE-based representations, each non-overlapping 2 2 latent block is concatenated along the channel dimension to form one patch feature before adaptive pooling. Representations that are already provided as patch-level features, such as Show-o2-7B and BLIP3-o-4B, are pooled directly from their native feature grids. This procedure standardizes the spatial grid without requiring RU and RG to have the same feature dimension. For the sensitivity metric, cosine similarity uses ϵcos = 106. sections.title: B COMPRESSION AND ALIGNMENT
sections.content: In Stage 1, we freeze the native understanding and generation pathways of the unified multimodal model and optimize only the GToken Encoder, Decoder, and their prediction heads. The GToken EncoderDecoder adopts symmetric six-layer Transformer architecture with hidden size of 1024, 8 attention heads, and 4096-dimensional FFN, together with 2D RoPE for spatial position encoding. The Encoder first projects the generation representation to 1024 dimensions and concatenates it with 256 learnable queries. Joint self-attention with spatial positional encoding then aggregates the generation information. The query outputs are subsequently projected to the hidden dimension of the corresponding understanding-pathway tokens, forming fixed-length generation memory G. During the latter half of training, we unfreeze the GToken Encoder and jointly optimize it with the projector, internal injection modules, and LoRA modules. The native visual encoders remain frozen throughout training. The projector maps the tokens to the corresponding understanding width and uses the same positional encoding scheme as the native understanding-side visual tokens. Each internal attention injection block uses the current-layer text hidden states in the understanding pathway as queries and projects the queries, keys, and values into 1024-dimensional, 16-head attention space. The retrieved features are passed through an output projection and residually written back to the text hidden states. Gradient decomposition. During training, we separately compute the gradients from the real/positive branch and the shuffle-G branch. The real/positive gradient contains the answer-CE gradient and the positive DPO gradient, while the shuffle-G branch produces the negative DPO gradient. The positive and negative DPO gradients are combined with weights of 4 : 1, respectively. The global norm of the negative gradient is then capped at 0.25 times that of the real/positive gradient, after which it is added to the real/positive gradient and the shuffle-G KL gradient. Finally, the combined gradient is clipped to maximum global norm of 1.0. Understanding-representation masking. To reduce reliance on the native understanding pathway during early training, we mask the complete understanding representation Ui for each sample with probability pU (t), while keeping the corresponding generation memory Gi, question, and answer unchanged. sections.title: D EXPERIMENTAL DETAILS
sections.content: D.1 DATA The compression and alignment stage uses 1M images sampled with stratification from Cambrian. For task-conditioned fine-tuning, we select 1,344,016 samples with relevance scores of at least 3 from the non-text-only subset of FineVision. VSR-Bench uses 7,680 training samples from its official random split and 2,195 samples from its official test split. For the medical-domain experiments, we use 19,654 training samples and 6,719 test samples from the official PathVQA splits. Representative examples from the three datasets are shown below. They illustrate fine-grained multiobject reasoning in FineVision, local spatial-relation recognition in VSR-Bench, and pathological visual question answering in PathVQA. 21 Training Data Example 1 (FineVision) FineVision: Multi-object reasoning Is the number of large things that are in front of the large Question: gray cylinder greater than the number of cyan metal cylinders behind the small brown thing? Answer: Fixed tissue. Figure 7: Fine-grained pathological example from PathVQA. D.2 TRAINING Stage 1: Compression and alignment. We use the AdamW optimizer with peak learning rate of 104, warmed up linearly over the first 200 optimizer steps. The learning rate then follows cosine decay schedule to minimum of 105. We set the weight decay to 0.01, β = (0.9, 0.95), ϵ = 108, and the maximum gradient norm to 1.0. Training uses 8 GPUs, with micro-batch size of 4 per GPU, an effective global batch size of 32, and 8,000 optimizer steps. Stage 2: Task-conditioned injection and fine-tuning. Training uses an effective global batch size of 32 for 5,000 optimizer steps. The injection projector and internal attention modules use peak learning rate of 2 105, while the understanding-pathway LoRA uses 104. Both learning rates are linearly warmed up over the first 500 optimizer steps and then follow cosine decay to 2 106 and 105, respectively. The LoRA rank and alpha are both set to 16. We use AdamW with weight decay of 0. To verify whether the model uses sample-specific tokens, we periodically evaluate the real branch and the shuffle-G branch on fixed validation subset. The real branch uses the matched generation memory Gi, whereas the shuffle-G branch replaces it with Gπ(i) while keeping the question, answer, and native understanding representation unchanged. Figure 8 reports the answer-token CE of the real and shuffle-G branches and their CE gap under three fine-tuning objectives: CE only, CE + DPO, and CE + DPO + KL. The CE gap is defined as CEshuffleG CEreal. The CE-only configuration maintains only small positive CE gap, indicating that the model makes limited use of sample-specific tokens. Introducing DPO explicitly optimizes the CE difference between matched and mismatched generation memory, encouraging the model to assign lower answertoken CE to the matched Gi and thereby increasing the CE gap. However, this objective may enlarge the gap by excessively degrading the shuffle-G branch. The shuffle-G KL regularization addresses this issue by constraining the output distribution of the shuffled branch to remain close to that of the frozen reference model, protecting the shuffled branch from uncontrolled deviation while preserving the positive CE gap. Thus, DPO promotes the use of sample-specific generation information, whereas KL regularization controls the cost of using mismatched generation memory. The three columns correspond to CE only, CE + DPO, and CE + DPO + KL, respectively. The first row reports the answer-token CE of the real and shuffle-G branches, while the second row reports their CE gap, defined as CEshuffleG CEreal. The real branch uses matched tokens, whereas the shuffle-G branch uses mismatched tokens from another sample. positive CE gap indicates that the model assigns lower answer-token cross-entropy to matched tokens. VStar-Bench: We use 191 multiple-choice samples and shuffle the option positions in the formal manifest. For each candidate answer, we compute the average answer-token CE and select the candidate with the lowest CE. Option labels are normalized to uppercase AD, and we report choice accuracy. OmniSpatial: We use 1,533 spatial-reasoning samples. The main protocol uses forcedchoice scoring based on the average candidate-token CE. For each candidate answer, we compute the average token CE and select the candidate with the lowest CE. MMVP: We use 300 questions forming 150 complementary question pairs. For each candidate answer, we compute the average token CE and select the candidate with the lowest CE. VSR-Bench: We use 2,195 samples from the random test split and apply the True/False greedy-generation protocol. PathVQA: We use all 6,719 samples from the official test set for medical visual question answering. We use greedy decoding without sampling until EOS is generated or the maximum number of new tokens is reached. We report normalized exact-match accuracy, where generated and reference answers are lowercased and stripped of punctuation before exact matching.

sections.title: E LIMITATIONS
sections.content: First, GAFU currently targets UMMs with mainstream dual-pathway visual encoders and does not cover all UMM architectures. Its application to models with different visual pathway designs or incompatible representation interfaces requires additional adaptation. Second, the effectiveness of GAFU depends on the quality of the native generation representations, and the resulting benefit may vary across models and tasks. Third, despite its performance gains, extracting, projecting, and injecting the generation tokens introduces extra inference computation and memory overhead compared with using the native understanding pathway alone.
